newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope urges Yeltsin to change text of religious law.
newsitem.headline: Pope urges Yeltsin to change text of religious law.

text.p: Pope John Paul forcefully told Russian President Boris Yeltsin on Thursday that a bill to curb the rights of minority religions in Russia threatened the survival of the Catholic Church there.
In a letter released by the Vatican, the Pontiff said he was "seriously worried" by the bill and urged Yeltsin to change it.
"This text...would constitute for the Catholic Church in Russia a real threat to the normal development of its pastoral activities and even its survival," he said.
The Pope is on holiday in the Italian Alps.
The bill, entitled "On Freedom of Conscience and Religious Association", has already been passed by Russia's parliament and must now be signed by Yeltsin for it to become law.
It would deny legal status to new religious groups for 15 years and give higher legal status to those religious organisations that have existed in Russia for 50 years.
Such a definition encompasses the Russian Orthodox Church, Jewish Islamic and Buddhist groups.
It would also impose new curbs on religious activities by foreign groups.
The Pope decried the fact that the bill excluded Catholicism from the "traditional religions" protected under the law and called for the "legitimate rights of believers" to be protected.

"Your Excellency will understand my worries and my fervent desire...that we can reach a new draft of a text which...would be a guarantor of religious peace in the great Russian nation," the letter said.
As the bill stood, the Pope said it appeared the authorities wanted to assimilate the Catholic Church into a foreign community with no consideration for its secular activities.
He said he was confident Yeltsin would "take the opportune decisions when the time comes".
Russian human rights activists have urged Yeltsin to veto the bill, saying it will inflame religious tensions.
Some religious activists opposed to the bill say those who would be stripped of their legal status include Catholics, Lutherans, Presbyterians, Methodists, Baptists, and Adventists.
The Russian Orthodox Church strongly supports the bill.
Relations between the Catholic and the Russian Orthodox Churches are at a low ebb.
The Orthodox have accused Catholics of using their new-found freedom in the former Soviet Union states to woo converts.

Shortly before an inter-religious conference in Austria last month, Patriarch Alexiy II of the Russian Orthodox Church called off a proposed meeting with the Pope. It would have been the first such meeting since the Great Schism split the Christian Churches into eastern and western branches in 1054.

Last month, for the first time in 21 years, the Orthodox Church did not send a delegation to an annual feast at the Vatican in representation of Ecumenical Patriarch of Istanbul, spiritual leader of the world's Orthodox Christians.
Better relations with the Orthodox Church would be essential if the Pope is to realise his dream of visiting Moscow to preach reconciliation and Christian unity.
Yeltsin has invited the Pope to visit Russia but the Pontiff cannot make the trip until the Russian Orthodox Church gives him the green light.
Religion has made a strong comeback in Russia since the collapse of atheistic communism after which all religions were made equal under the country's post-Soviet constitution.
But human rights activists fear the bill signals a return to Soviet-style repression and discrimination.
The U.S. Senate voted earlier this week to cut off aid to Russia if Yeltsin signed the measure.
